items.title: D'Imperio interviewed by Monk Rowe, 2014
items.q: Jake, the three drummers, with me, Jake Hanna and Don Lamond. I’ve got a picture of the three of us together. We shared the drum chairs on that.

ctx.x: I agree. I mean I made four dollars on my first gig. But I made 35 dollars on my first New Year’s Eve gig when I was still in high school and I said, “oh my God.” But I think it’s interesting that your father said, “you overplayed that break.”

Like in other words, at the end of the tune — the LP was coming in at that time. Between 1949 — I think Columbia was the originator of the long playing record. They used to be on ten inches. But there was two records that I remember particularly on that table when we moved to Cortland here, was Harry James’ “One Night Stand,” and he had a drummer named Jackie Mills who absolutely floored me. But what was even more impressive, or as impressive, was a Ted Heath record called “Live at the London Palladium” and the…

Yeah. Were you developing, by the time you were in your teens and so forth, any kind of personal filter — oh I really want to play this kind of music and I don’t care for this kind of music too much. Or was it just like a gig is a gig?
